Self-service
In the platform, self-service should provide functions for users to make and fulfill requests
independently, while also allowing multiple functional teams of the platform to self-extend
according to their respective work requirements. In this process, relevant self-service capabilities
can be provided as needed, allowing users to choose themselves and minimizing manual
intervention as much as possible.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

Chapter 6 187
In the software delivery process, the self-service platform enables developers to directly manage
and operate resources and handle resource lifecycle management, without having to pay attention
to the technical architecture of the underlying infrastructure and the implementation details of
resource output, while also reducing direct intervention from platform team members. This self-
service model follows the principle of “those who build, manage,” but does not require developers
to deeply understand underlying technologies.
From a collaboration perspective, self-service is more like a combination of process and tool. On
the tooling level, whether it’s open-source software or commercial software, they all provide
abstractions for general capabilities; but at the process level, due to different management
requirements and dependencies in the collaborative processes of various enterprises, there will
be differences in process design. Therefore, tools can be standardized, but processes are difficult
to standardize.
Let me give an example. In different projects, workplaces, and team contexts, different strategies
need to be formulated according to the development habits of developers, so that developers can
self-serve when operating the infrastructure, as shown in Figure 6.10.
Figure 6.10: Integration methods of self-service in infrastructure
The first approach is to create an infrastructure library that represents infrastructure resources
and configuration information, allowing users to freely use their preferred deployment tools for
infrastructure configuration.
The second approach is to create a command-line interface (CLI) for the infrastructure, enabling
developers to manage and orchestrate infrastructure through a familiar CLI.
The third approach is to create an infrastructure platform application, providing developers
with a graphical user interface (GUI) to configure and manage the infrastructure.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 188
All these methods have one thing in common: they adopt a standardized architecture, which
includes best practices defined by the platform team, mechanisms for enforcing deployment
rules, and a unified deployment workflow (such as code review, pull requests, CI/CD, testing, etc.).
Reducing user cognitive load
During platform development, reducing user cognitive load is a key factor that is easily overlooked.
To mitigate risks to the team caused by excessive cognitive load, the platform should encapsulate
tool implementation details and hide infrastructure complexity. For example, some third-party
platforms provide integration services but require that detailed information not be exposed, so
the platform needs to handle this encapsulation. At the same time, the platform should also
meet the need for observability of certain services, which may require protocol conversion or

chunks.heading: Chapter 6 187

secondary processing of services.
Once the key attributes of an effective platform are clear, it becomes easier to examine the
concrete modules that usually make up a platform engineering system. These modules provide
the infrastructure, development tools, data services, security controls, operational capabilities,
and service marketplace functions that allow delivery teams to work more efficiently.
Core modules of platform engineering
The specific functional modules of platform engineering may vary depending on application
scenarios and customer requirements, but usually include the following core modules:
• Infrastructure: Includes the management and allocation of computing, storage, network,
and other infrastructure resources, as well as providing highly available and scalable
infrastructure services
• Development Tools: Includes tools for application development, testing, building, and
deployment, as well as developer portals, component libraries, documentation repositories,
and other tools and resources supporting developers
• Data Management: Includes data storage, data analysis, data backup and recovery services,
as well as data services supporting data integration and transformation
• Security and Identity Management: Includes security management services such
as authentication, authorization, encryption, and security audit, as well as services
supporting security policy and compliance management
• Operations and Maintenance Management: Includes services for application monitoring,
fault management, automated operations and maintenance, and services supporting
deployment and update management

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

Chapter 6 189
• Service Marketplace: Includes a service marketplace providing third-party applications,
services, and solutions, as well as services supporting application integration and
subscription
In addition, platform engineering can also include other functional modules, such as supporting
services in fields like artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things, to meet different application
scenarios and user needs.
After identifying the main modules that a platform may provide, the next step is to define the
capabilities required to build, operate, secure, and continuously improve those modules. These
capability requirements help translate the platform’s design into practical responsibilities for
platform teams and supporting roles.
Platform engineering capabilities
Typically, platform engineering capabilities can be specified from five aspects: platform
construction, platform services, platform operations, platform assurance, and platform team,
as shown in Figure 6.11.
Figure 6.11: Platform Engineering capability requirements
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 190
These requirements can be read as a practical checklist for designing and operating an internal
developer platform. They cover not only the services exposed to users, but also the construction,
operation, assurance, and team responsibilities needed to keep the platform useful and reliable
over time.
Platform service capability requirements
Platform service capability requirements describe what the platform must provide directly to
developers and delivery teams during everyday work. These requirements cover the services
users interact with most often, including development environments, coding support, API testing,
environment generation, self-testing, and CI/CD feedback. When a development environment
is needed, the platform should provide a secure development environment service, including an
IDE, environment configuration, and other development tools.

Where to start
For teams beginning their platform engineering journey, the first priority should be
the capabilities that create immediate value for platform users. Start with platform
service capabilities, such as secure development environments, reusable compo -
nents, CI/CD feedback, environment generation, and developer self-service. These
are the user-facing functions that help teams experience the platform as a useful
product rather than an additional process.
Next, focus on platform construction capabilities, including integration, extensi -
bility, unified access, security, compatibility with the existing technology stack, and
reliable infrastructure. These capabilities provide the technical foundation needed
to make the platform consistent and scalable.
Platform operation, assurance, and team capabilities can mature gradually as adop -

tion grows. Over the first 12–18 months, teams can strengthen user support, platform
reliability, security assurance, usage analytics, and dedicated platform roles. This
staged approach aligns with the idea that platform teams should evolve around
user needs, reduce cognitive load, and treat the platform as a product that improves
over time.
This staged approach is consistent with the platform-team guidance in Team Topol -
ogies by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, particularly its discussion of platform
teams and team cognitive load.

Beyond the services exposed to users, the platform also needs strong construction capabilities.
These requirements define how the platform itself should be built, integrated, standardized,
secured, and maintained so that it can support delivery teams reliably at scale.
Platform construction capability requirements
The following requirements describe the construction principles that help make the platform
extensible, secure, consistent, performant, and compatible with the organization’s existing
technology environment:
• Platform construction should highlight integration and extensibility, such as easy
integration with other tools, plugin marketplaces, etc.
• Platform construction should emphasize unified management dimensions, such as using
applications as the central management objects of the platform.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 193
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 193
• Platform construction should reflect a single, trusted source for basic data to avoid
duplicated maintenance, such as user information and application information.
• Platform construction should feature unified portal design, including unified entry point,
unified account, unified permissions, etc.
• Platform construction should reflect unified interaction design, such as unified interface
style, unified operation methods, unified terminology, etc.
• Platform construction should comply with applicable national procurement and data
sovereignty requirements, including the environment, middleware, databases, components,
and other tools on which platform development and operation depend.
• Platform construction should demonstrate ease of use, such as user guides, simplified
operation steps, error prompts, etc.
• Platform construction should demonstrate configurability and manageability, such as
template configuration, management rule maintenance, etc.
• Platform construction should demonstrate security, such as avoiding uncontrolled public
accounts and uncontrolled build machine administrator privileges.
• Platform construction should demonstrate high performance, such as load balancing,
building resource pools, caching, etc.
• Platform construction should demonstrate high quality, such as few functional defects, etc.
• Platform construction should demonstrate availability and stability, such as active-active
deployment, etc.
• Platform construction should demonstrate compatibility with the organization’s internal
technology stack and infrastructure, such as supporting different programming languages
and different resource types.
• Platform construction should demonstrate compatibility of functional versions, reducing
the impact of version updates on users. Platform construction should demonstrate
openness and standardization, such as providing external service invocation capability
via APIs, etc.
• Development, testing, operations, and other activities during the platform construction
process should also be managed using the platform’s own services.
Once the platform has been built, it must also be operated as a living product. Platform operation
capability requirements focus on user support, adoption, feedback, usage analysis, communication,
and continuous improvement.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 194
Platform operational capability requirements
The following requirements describe how the platform should be supported, promoted, measured,
and improved after it is released to users:
• Platform operations should establish basic user support mechanisms, such as user
discussion groups, expert guidance, user manuals, and training
• Platform operations should establish automated user support mechanisms, such as
automated customer service

• Platform operations should establish user promotion and publicity mechanisms, such
as posting announcements, new feature promotional activities, release frequency, and
new user promotions
• Platform operations should establish user demand collection and feedback mechanisms
• Platform operations should establish notification and display mechanisms for platform
availability, such as the duration of function recovery
• Platform operations should have reasonable user usage billing models and optimization
mechanisms
• Platform operations should have statistical analyses of user usage and operation status,
such as number of users, usage coverage, availability rate, and feature usage frequency
• Platform operations should have statistical analyses of user usage effectiveness, such as
data on organizational efficiency improvement
In addition to operation, the platform also needs assurance capabilities to protect its reliability,
security, availability, and release safety. These requirements are especially important because
the platform becomes a shared dependency for many delivery teams.
Platform assurance capability requirements
The following requirements describe the stability, security, high availability, data protection, and
low-risk release practices needed to keep the platform dependable:
• The platform should adopt stability and security assurance mechanisms for relatively
important business systems, such as SLA setting, monitoring and early warning, emergency
plans, change processes, and security scanning mechanisms
• The platform should adopt high-availability assurance measures for applications, such
as load balancing, call relationship management, and failover

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

chunks.content:
Chapter 6 195
• The platform should adopt high-availability assurance measures for data, such as database
and table partitioning, read-write separation, real-time local backup, and offsite backup
• The platform should employ low-risk deployment and release strategies, such as canary
(gray) releases
• The platform should have operations and security personnel responsible for ensuring the
stability and security of the platform
Finally, platform engineering depends on the team responsible for building, operating, and
evolving the platform. Platform team capability requirements define the roles needed to manage
the platform as both a technical system and an internal product.
Platform team capability requirements
The following requirements describe the main roles that may be needed in a platform team,
including product management, operations, architecture, development, testing, security, and
technical coaching:
• There should be a physical or virtual platform team responsible for the overall construction,
assurance, and promotional operations of the platform
• The platform team should include the role of platform product manager, responsible for
platform planning and requirements management
• The platform team should include the role of platform product operations, responsible
for platform promotional operations
• The platform team should include the role of platform architect, responsible for platform
architecture design, such as feature distribution, performance, and high availability
• The platform team should include the role of platform development and testing, responsible
for platform development and quality assurance
• The platform team should include the role of platform operations and security, responsible
for platform stability and security
• The platform team may include the role of platform technical coach, responsible for
technical services related to the platform
After defining the platform’s required services, construction principles, operating model,
assurance practices, and team roles, the next question is how organizations should adopt platform
engineering in practice. The following best practices show how teams can start small, treat the
platform as a product, and connect tool libraries with knowledge bases.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 196
Best practices for platform engineering
Platform engineering does not need to begin as a large, centralized transformation program. In
many organizations, it starts by improving a small but painful part of the delivery workflow, then
gradually expands as teams see value and provide feedback.
Practice platform engineering anytime, anywhere
Platform engineering can be practiced anytime, anywhere. We usually start with easily achievable
goals. For example, in a certain project, if a development team is already using common

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 195
chunks.content:
development tools, those tools can be integrated into the platform as the first batch of services
offered.
Next, the platform architect should collect platform engineering requirements from the platform
users, usually through interviews or surveys to understand current problems with their tool usage,
what obstacles the tools create for the development teams, and what the most challenging issues
are for them, such as helping manage container clusters or orchestrate deployment processes.
It should be noted that completing the platform engineering build entirely in a closed-off manner,
from scratch to production, can cause obstacles during rollout. For example, if you tell the delivery
team that, for technical stack considerations, all tools need to be standardized and unified,
and require them to abandon their current tools and switch all delivery work to the platform
engineering tools, this approach will only add more tasks for the delivery personnel. The purpose
of platform engineering is to enhance collaboration, not to reduce efficiency—unless you can
prove that the platform actually makes their work easier and more efficient.
Therefore, best practices for platform engineering should be conducted anytime, anywhere, and
centered around engineering culture.
Platform engineering is a product with a lifecycle
Regarding best practices for platform engineering, you should start with a small, easy-to-achieve
goal—one that can bring quantifiable value to the team or a specific node in the software delivery
process at minimal cost. For example, during software delivery, when developers or teams use
outdated technologies in a release, technology iteration can rarely be completed all at once, nor
can all work be directly migrated to platform engineering. When promoting the platform, platform
architects should first consider the current state of the delivery teams, choose appropriate delivery
methods, ways to collaborate with other teams, the technology stack in use, and the tools being
used, to help them gradually transition from their current state to the ideal state.

Take IDP as an example, it must be clear that IDP is not a one-time project. More often, IDP
serves the majority of users involved in software delivery. Therefore, a mature IDP is a service
that can continuously iterate. The platform needs to continually provide services, new tools, and
combinations of tools. Platform engineering is a product with a lifecycle that requires continuous
iteration and operation.
The logic of tool libraries and knowledge bases
A tool cluster is also known as a tool library. An excellent tool library can provide a good working
experience for delivery personnel throughout the entire R&D ecosystem. Platform engineering
has clear requirements for how to create an integrated and unified developer experience, which
directly affects the satisfaction of the platform’s core users—developers. Therefore, optimizing
the tool experience and making it process-oriented and integrated is an important measure to
improve the developer experience.
The knowledge base is what supports tool usage and determines the specific execution logic.
Here, knowledge is not limited to static carriers such as documents and charts but should also
include dynamic carriers such as rules, processes, views, queries, and models. The form of the
carrier is determined by its method of consumption. The essence of a platform is knowledge, and
only knowledge that has been validated in practice can guarantee its reliability and value. Teams
should try to solidify knowledge into the platform and efficiently, stably, and comprehensively
practice and validate knowledge through integration with the tool library. Only in this way can
knowledge continue to accumulate and iterate, thereby producing economies of scale, coping
with unknown challenges, and accelerating the rate at which value is realized.
As shown in Figure 6.12, the knowledge base drives the tool library, promoting continuous
optimization of infrastructure, R&D processes, and environment management. The tool library
also feeds back to the knowledge base, continuously supplementing business, architecture, and
technical knowledge.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 198
Figure 6.12: The drive and feedback relationship between the knowledge base and the tool
library
After examining how platform engineering is designed and adopted, it is useful to clarify how it
relates to the other two delivery disciplines discussed in this chapter: DevOps and SRE. These
disciplines overlap in tools and goals, but they serve different primary audiences and solve different
delivery problems.
Differences between platform engineering, DevOps, and
SRE
After examining platform engineering concepts, capabilities, and best practices, it is useful to
clarify how platform engineering relates to the other two delivery disciplines discussed in this

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 197
chunks.content:
chapter: DevOps and SRE. These practices overlap in tools and goals, but they serve different
primary audiences and solve different delivery problems.
Differences from DevOps
DevOps is a way to transform the culture of collaboration into system lifecycle management
(SDLC), a concept aimed at improving software delivery speed and quality. DevOps promotes
collaboration and communication between development and operations teams, and accelerates
automation to streamline deployment. Platform engineering is a practice rather than a
methodology, and can be regarded as the next iteration of DevOps, as it shares DevOps’ principles
of collaboration, continuous improvement, and automation.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 199
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 199
There are differences between platform teams and DevOps in some respects. DevOps uses tools
and automation to simplify the process of code release, management, and observation through
logging and monitoring tools, with a primary focus on building efficient CI/CD pipelines. Platform
engineers use all the tools that DevOps uses and integrate them into a shared platform for use
across IT teams at the enterprise level. This reduces the need for teams to individually configure
and manage infrastructure and tools, saving significant time, effort, and resources. Platform
engineers are also responsible for creating documentation and optimizing the platform so that
developers can use tools and infrastructure self-servingly in their workflows.
Only mature companies with multiple IT teams using complex tools and infrastructures need
a platform team. In such engineering environments, a dedicated platform team is typically
required to manage the complexity. The platform team is responsible for building and managing
infrastructure and helping DevOps accelerate continuous delivery. However, in startups, DevOps
teams often also take on platform engineering tasks.
Differences from SRE
SRE focuses on ensuring applications are reliable, secure, and always available. They work with
developers and operations teams to create systems or infrastructure that support the delivery
of highly reliable applications. SREs also perform capacity planning, infrastructure scaling, and
incident management and response to ensure that the platform meets the required service level
objectives. In addition, platform engineering manages complex infrastructure and builds efficient
platforms for developers to optimize the SDLC. Although both work on the platform and their
roles sound similar, their goals are different.
The main difference between platform teams and SREs is in whom they serve and how they
serve them. SREs face end users and ensure that applications are reliable and available for them.
Platform engineers are oriented toward internal developers, focusing on improving the developer
experience. The daily tasks of the two teams differ in relation to these goals. Platform engineering
provides the underlying infrastructure for rapid application delivery, while SREs do the same for
delivering highly reliable and available applications. SREs are more focused on troubleshooting
and incident response, while platform engineers focus on complex infrastructure and support
for developer self-service.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 200
In order to achieve their respective goals, SRE and platform teams use different tools in their
workflows. SREs mainly use monitoring and logging tools like Prometheus or Grafana to detect
anomalies in real time and set up automatic alerts. Platform teams use a different set of tools that

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 199
chunks.content:
span various stages of the software delivery process, such as container orchestration tools, CI/CD
pipeline tools, and IaC tools. Overall, SREs and platform teams are committed to building reliable
and scalable infrastructures, with different goals, but there is some overlap in the tools they use.
Once the relationship between platform engineering, DevOps, and SRE is clear, the final step is to
consider how platform engineering changes in the era of LLMs. LLMs can extend internal platforms
by improving requirements analysis, developer assistance, knowledge retrieval, automation, and
operational insight.
Platform engineering under LLMs
Driven by LLMs, the development and application of platform engineering have become more
efficient and flexible. By combining the powerful computational capabilities of these models
with platform engineering, organizations can better achieve automation, standardization, and
scalability. In this process, platform engineering is not just about building and maintaining
infrastructure, but also about holistic optimization of the entire development process.
Furthermore, platform engineering leverages the intelligent analytical capabilities of LLMs for
more precise performance monitoring and optimization. By processing and analyzing large
volumes of data, platforms can automatically identify potential bottlenecks and issues, propose
solutions, and help organizations improve operational efficiency.
Challenges encountered in platform engineering
According to the latest report released by CloudBees, Platform Engineering 2023: Rapid Adoption
and Impact, 83% of respondents have either fully implemented platform engineering or are at
some stage of implementation. According to the data in the report, developers actually spend
only 12.5% to 30% of their weekly time writing code. This has prompted IT organization leaders
to urgently seek new ways to improve developer productivity; therefore, the need for innovative
technologies in platform engineering is pressing, especially machine learning technologies and
LLM technologies.
Firstly, as enterprise data continues to accumulate, data privacy, and security become increasingly
important, especially in LLM scenarios. For training data in specific domains, this inevitably brings
challenges to traditional platform engineering. Especially in managing multiple large datasets
and models, platform engineering needs to integrate machine learning algorithms and LLMs.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 201
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 201
Secondly, platform engineering must adapt to new AI workflows and data, prompts, as well as
the pipelines for AI engineers who design, train, and maintain models, vector databases, and
large datasets—all of which will continue to grow and evolve. These AI pipelines must support
the specific requirements of their workflow patterns and align with interdependent software
development pipelines and release processes.
Finally, with changes in enterprise business models, more and more business systems are adopting
GPUs, VPUs, and highly scalable CPUs to process large amounts of data. This approach also poses
challenges to traditional platform engineering. In order to enable the platform to play a greater
role, platform engineering needs to proactively incorporate more innovative technologies.
Common practice methods
Since platform engineering is mainly aimed at internal enterprise developers, business
requirements—as an upstream point in the development process—need extra attention. Likewise,
the developers’ own tools also need to be considered.
Automated enhancement, analysis, and conversion of business
requirements
In terms of automated requirements enhancement, platform engineering, combined with LLM
technology, can analyze user feedback and data to automatically identify and supplement missing
requirement information. For example, it can automatically identify user-raised issues and convert
them into requirement descriptions, and automatically complete requirement keywords and tags.
In automated requirements analysis, domain knowledge obtained through data training can
better evaluate and optimize requirements, uncover potential problems and opportunities, and
improve the efficiency and effectiveness of requirements analysis.
In automated requirements convergence, by leveraging LLM technologies such as intelligent
recommendations, conversational systems, and multi-party collaboration, developers can
communicate and collaborate more effectively, collect and integrate user feedback and pain
points more effectively, and improve satisfaction and consistency of requirements.
Smarter development tools
Based on the existing functionality of development tools, it is necessary to integrate more
capabilities from the software delivery process, such as automated code review, automated testing,
automated log analysis, and AI-assisted programming. This significantly improves developers’
efficiency and provides an excellent user experience.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 202
At the same time, based on LLM capabilities, development tools can also analyze documents
and code generated during development, build knowledge bases, and provide intelligent Q&A
capabilities for developers, thus simplifying learning costs for developers and reducing users’

chunks.heading: Chapter 6 201
chunks.content:
cognitive load.
Platform engineering helps internal teams deliver software more efficiently by providing reusable
tools, infrastructure, workflows, and self-service capabilities. However, efficient delivery is only
one part of modern software engineering. The next section turns to Site Reliability Engineering,
which focuses on keeping systems reliable, scalable, observable, and resilient once they are running
in production.
Strengthening system reliability with SRE
Site Reliability Engineering extends modern software delivery by focusing on the reliability,
scalability, performance, and operability of systems after they are designed, built, and released.
While DevOps improves collaboration and delivery flow, and platform engineering provides
reusable internal platforms, SRE applies software engineering practices to operational problems
such as availability, monitoring, incident response, build reliability, change risk, and go-live
assurance. This section explains how SRE emerged, what goals it serves, how SRE teams can be
organized, and how SRE practices help teams design, deliver, and operate more reliable systems.
For relevant SRE system content, refer to the SRE Practice White Paper.
Origin of SRE
In 2003, Google launched a brand-new team, namely the SRE team, aiming to improve the
reliability of application systems through software engineering approaches. As SRE theories and
practices gradually matured within Google, SRE practices were gradually expanded to the entire
industry. Since the introduction of the SRE concept, it has attracted the attention and imitation
of many enterprises. However, the methods of implementing SRE vary among enterprises, and
the effectiveness of SRE implementation also differs.
Goals of SRE
The primary goal of SRE is to improve the reliability, scalability, performance, and efficiency of
large-scale distributed systems by combining best practices from software engineering and system
operations, as well as enhancing monitoring, alerting, and fault recovery capabilities.
• Reliability: The foremost goal of SRE is to ensure the reliability of services and systems.
This includes reducing failures and increasing system stability to ensure that users can
consistently receive high-quality services at all times.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 203
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 203
• Scalability: SRE is committed to designing and implementing systems that can scale with
growing user demands. This involves optimizing system architecture and resources to
handle fluctuations in real workloads without sacrificing performance.
• Performance: SRE focuses on system performance, aiming to ensure that systems can
respond to user requests quickly within a reasonable timeframe. This includes continuous
monitoring and optimization of system bottlenecks to enhance overall performance.
• Efficiency: SRE advocates for automating operational tasks to reduce human error and
improve efficiency. Through automation, new features can be deployed more rapidly,
failures can be detected and responded to faster, and system upgrades and maintenance
can be conducted more reasonably.
• Monitoring and Alerting: SRE emphasizes comprehensive monitoring of systems to detect
and resolve problems in a timely manner. By setting up effective alerting systems, rapid
response to major issues can be achieved before they impact users, thereby minimizing
user impact.
• Fault Recovery Capability: SRE stresses quickly and effectively restoring services to
minimize interruptions to user experience. This includes developing and rehearsing
emergency response plans for critical situations.
The process by which enterprises achieve the core goals of SRE is not uniform, and implementation
paths vary. SRE-related practices exist within many workflows and are independent of the form
or organizational location of SRE departments or teams within a company. These workflows
are closely integrated with R&D, testing, operations, and product operations teams, with every
participating team contributing to the aforementioned SRE goals.
With these reliability goals established, the next step is to look at the practical mission of the SRE
team within an organization.
Mission of the SRE team
The main purpose of having an SRE team within an organization is to ensure the reliability and
efficient operation of systems. By introducing the SRE role, organizations can better balance the
needs between software development speed and system stability, thereby achieving a higher level
of availability, performance, and automation. The mission of the SRE team within the organization
is as follows.
• Reliability First: The SRE team is committed to ensuring high availability and reliability
of services. They focus on system stability and adopt an engineering approach to reduce
failures and improve system robustness.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 204
• Automated Operations: The SRE team promotes automated operations to reduce manual
errors and improve efficiency. Through automation, deployments, monitoring, fault
detection, and restoration can be performed more quickly and reliably.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 203
chunks.content:
• Quality Assurance: The SRE team participates in the entire service lifecycle, including
design, development, deployment, and maintenance stages, to ensure the system
maintains high quality at every stage.
• Rapid Innovation: By reducing failures and increasing system stability, the SRE team
provides the development team with a more stable platform, enabling them to focus more
on business innovation and the development of new features.
Because organizations differ in size, structure, and operational maturity, SRE teams can be
organized in different ways. The next subsection introduces the most common team models
and explains how each model supports reliability work.
Forms of SRE team presence
In organizational structures, the form in which SRE teams exist can vary, primarily depending
on the organization’s size, business needs, and culture. The following are some common forms
of SRE team presence:
• Centralized SRE Team: A dedicated SRE team is responsible for supporting the reliability
efforts of the entire organization. This model helps concentrate expertise and ensures the
consistent implementation of best practices organization-wide.
• Embedded SRE Team: SRE team members are embedded within various product or service
teams, working closely with development teams. This model helps integrate reliability
efforts into the entire product development process.
• Hybrid Model: Some organizations adopt a hybrid model, establishing both a centralized
SRE team and embedding SRE roles within some key projects. This model leverages the
advantages of both specialization and close business integration.
Each form has its own advantages and applicable scenarios, and the most suitable model can be
chosen according to organizational needs. Regardless of the form, the goal of SRE is to enhance
system reliability and efficiency through automation and engineering approaches.
As shown in Figure 6.13, the SRE engineering group adopts a centralized setup, responsible for
the construction and promotion of the SRE system. This group drives the SRE platform R&D
group and the infrastructure group, providing highly efficient tools and platform products to
improve the reliability of foundational services.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 205
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 205
Figure 6.13: Centralized SRE organization
As shown in Figure 6.14, each SRE team adopts an embedded setup, responsible for the construction
and promotion of the SRE system within each business division, and is in charge of collecting
business requirements and abstracting these requirements into capabilities.
Figure 6.14: Embedded SRE organization
After defining SRE goals and team structures, the next step is to examine how SRE practices are
applied during system design. Reliability is not achieved only through incident response after
a system is running; it must be built into the architecture through design choices that reduce
failure impact and improve recovery.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 206
Application resilient architecture
Application resilient architecture is a very important part of reliability architecture. It refers
to adopting highly reliable architecture design solutions such as distributed design, decoupled
design, and redundancy design according to the reliability requirements of the system during
the system architecture design process, in order to improve system reliability. The full lifecycle
practice process of reliability engineering is shown in Figure 6.15.
Figure 6.15: Full lifecycle practice process of reliability engineering
In the process of reliability architecture design, the SRE team needs to fully integrate into the
application architecture design process, and jointly participate in architecture design and review
with the R&D team. In the system design stage, potential single points of failure, capacity, and
other latent risks should be eliminated as much as possible, and emergency preparations should
be made in advance for possible system architecture risks.
Distributed design
The system has components with clear responsibilities, appropriate granularity, and easy
management, such as computing resources, business modules, and data. These components
can be deployed and run in a distributed manner. Components are independent and do not
interfere with each other. Distributed design can improve development efficiency and system
reliability. Component splitting can be achieved through replication, vertical splitting according
to functionality, or horizontal splitting based on users or access patterns.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 207
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 207
During design, possible mutual interference between components should be fully considered, as
well as how to balance the load between different components, distributing the system’s load
evenly to mitigate negative impacts on overall performance.
Decoupled design
In the architecture design process, various logical functions can be divided into different service
modules, ensuring that failures in one module have minimal impact on other modules, thereby
minimizing the coupling degree between modules. In this way, the system can be divided into
multiple independent functional modules. It is worth noting that the main business logic is
independent from other non-core modules, so failures in non-core business modules do not
negatively affect the core functions of the business.
Redundancy
To ensure that resources have a sufficient safety margin, each component needs to have enough
and reasonable redundant instances to ensure that the failure of a single component instance does
not affect normal business operations. For different types of components, we need to clearly define
the amount and type of redundancy. In practice, when device failures or improper operations
cause server performance degradation or crashes, the system will enter an abnormal state and
generate a large amount of information. Applications may be deployed across multiple data
centers, and when data redundancy exists between these centers, errors at one location can be
corrected using data from another, ensuring continuity and reliability of the entire system. To
enhance system reliability, read-write separation is often used for data redundancy management.
Read-write separation is a form of redundancy design in which data redundancy exists between
the cache and the database. When the cache service goes down, data can be backfilled from the
database to the cache.
Circuit breaker
The circuit breaker mechanism is a microservices protection mechanism used to address the
avalanche effect. If the target service responds slowly or there are too many timeouts, the calls
to that service will be cut off (circuit broken). Subsequent calls will no longer attempt to invoke
the target service; instead, a predefined result will be returned directly, allowing resources to be
quickly freed. Generally, circuit breakers require different recovery strategies. If the condition of
the target service improves, normal requests can resume.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 208
Rate limiting
Rate limiting is a system design technique used to control access traffic to applications or services
and to prevent resource overload. Common rate limiting strategies include fixed window, sliding
log, leaky bucket, and token bucket algorithms. These strategies help the system cope with
high traffic, maintaining stability and reliability. In practice, rate limiting is often combined with

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 207
chunks.content:
other protective measures such as queues, caching, service degradation, and circuit breaking, to
achieve comprehensive traffic control and system protection. When traffic is limited, the system
usually rejects excess requests, queues requests for later processing, returns an error code (such
as HTTP 429 Too Many Requests), or provides a degraded service response, effectively alleviating
server pressure.
Degradation
Degradation mechanisms are used when server pressure surges; based on current business
and traffic conditions, specific services and pages are strategically degraded to relieve server
resource pressure, free up resources, and ensure the normal operation of core tasks. Based on the
configuration, degradation can be divided into proactive and automatic degradation. Proactive
degradation is configured in advance, whereas automatic degradation executes when system
failures occur, such as timeouts or frequent failures. Automatic degradation can be further
subdivided into timeout degradation, failure-count degradation, and error degradation.
Observability
To ensure system transparency and quickly locate issues, adopting an observable design approach
is particularly crucial. Observability design encompasses several aspects, including logging, real-
time monitoring, tracing, and metrics, achieving measurable and analyzable system state and
behavior. In observability design, logs should record all key events in detail; monitoring systems
must capture critical performance metrics in real-time; tracing mechanisms should be able to track
requests across services; and metrics should comprehensively reflect the system’s health status.
Additionally, health check mechanisms should automatically assess the status of system
components, and, if abnormal metrics appear, the alerting mechanism will immediately notify
relevant personnel. With these measures, we can clearly observe the system’s operating state,
thus laying a solid foundation for subsequent maintenance and optimization.
Resilient architecture reduces the likelihood and impact of production failures, but system
reliability also depends on the reliability of the software delivery process itself. In CI/CD
environments, the build process must be fast, repeatable, and dependable so that teams can
release and verify changes safely.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 209
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 209
Build reliability
Build refers to the process of compiling and packaging source files such as code and resource
files into executable program files on a build machine. In the current continuous integration/
continuous delivery (CI/CD) software development model, if a problem occurs during the build,
the new software version cannot be quickly released and verified, which affects software quality.
Therefore, build reliability plays an important role in the reliability of software services and
iteration efficiency. Build reliability design mainly consists of two aspects: build efficiency and
build success rate.
Build efficiency
Build efficiency refers to build speed, determined by the time elapsed from the start to the end of
the build. If the build time is too long, the software version cannot be delivered on time, affecting
the iteration efficiency of business versions, and the reliability of the build is difficult to guarantee.
The main measures to improve build efficiency are as follows.
• Process automation: Use automated build tools or scripts to connect each build step,
reducing waiting time between steps.
• Parallelization: Optimize the process by changing parts of the build flow from serial to
parallel, thereby increasing build speed.
• Incremental build: When executing a build on the build machine, some temporary files
and intermediate products generated during the build are saved as build cache. During
the next build, since usually only part of the code has been modified, the unmodified code
can directly use the previous build cache, thus avoiding redundant builds. Incremental
builds reduce the content that needs to be built, thereby decreasing build time. To address
the lack of cache during the first build on the build machine, a build cache sharing server
can be set up (such as the DDC server for the UE engine). The build cache from one build
machine is uploaded to the shared cache server for use by other build machines.
• Distributed compilation: Compared to the limited resources of a single machine, the
power of a cluster is undoubtedly stronger: it is easy to see the difference between one
person computing 100 math problems and 100 people of the same ability each solving
one problem. Distributed compilation utilizes cluster resources, assigning the work of
a single node to a large number of nodes, and then aggregating the results. Depending
on requirements, the number of resources can be almost infinitely expanded, no longer
constrained by the physical architecture of a single machine; in terms of time, the time
required for a cluster to work is often only a fraction of the original time.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 210
• Software-hardware collaboration: Some build tasks (such as code preprocessing, resource

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 209
chunks.content:
file processing) cannot be accelerated for remote distribution via distributed compilation
and can only be processed on the local build machine. In this case, the local build machine’s
performance becomes the bottleneck. To address this, the CPU, memory, and disk IO
performance of the local build machine can be specifically enhanced. Combined with the
distributed compilation system, software and hardware collaborate to improve build speed.
• Multi-process compilation: Some compilation software defaults to single-process
compilation, resulting in underutilization of build machine hardware performance. In
this case, enabling multi-process compilation can improve build speed.
After identifying the main ways to improve build efficiency, teams also need methods for measuring
whether those improvements are working.
Evaluation methods for build efficiency
By improving build efficiency through the above methods, it is also necessary to evaluate the
effectiveness of builds. There are several evaluation methods as follows:
• Evaluation based on baseline: The effectiveness of a single build can be evaluated using
the proportion of build time exceeding the baseline. After each build is completed normally,
the build time is reported. After several days of continuous builds, a set of stable build time
data over a given period is collected. The average of these data points becomes the build
time baseline for that period. If a build’s duration exceeds the baseline by a significant
amount (e.g., 20%), there may be performance issues. Once the build time baseline is
established, the current build time can be compared to the baseline as an SLO (Service
Level Objective), such as considering it healthy if it does not exceed the baseline by more
than 10%.
• Evaluation based on threshold � Different thresholds can be set according to actual
business needs, for example, setting the build time not to exceed 2 hours as a measure
of reliability.
Build speed is only one part of build reliability; teams must also ensure that builds complete
successfully and consistently.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 211
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 211
Build success rate
Build success rate refers to the proportion of successful builds out of the total number of builds
within a specified time period. If the build success rate is low, multiple builds are required to
generate a deliverable version. The build success rate is one of the key factors affecting build
reliability. The main measures to improve the build success rate are as follows:
• Ensuring the reliability of the build environment: Build success rate is affected by
the build environment. If abnormalities occur on the build machine (such as missing
dependency packages, inability to connect to the code repository, disk failures, etc.), the
build will fail. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure the reliability of the build environment,
for example, by automating the large-scale deployment of build machines to avoid missing
dependencies caused by manual deployment, and by utilizing highly reliable network,
computing, and storage resources in cloud environments as much as possible.
• Pre-compilation checks: The build process usually executes compilation after pulling
the code, which requires developers to submit the code to the repository once they finish
coding in order to trigger the build process. In practice, issues can be exposed before the
code is committed to the repository. The earlier problems are discovered, the lower the cost
to fix them; the higher the quality of code committed to the repository, the fewer issues
there are, and the smoother and more efficient team collaboration will be. Pre-compilation
tools can, before code submission, run local pre-build checks or remote pre-compilation
checks to detect problems early, thus shifting quality to the left.
Once build success rate has been improved through environment reliability and pre-compilation
checks, it also needs to be measured against a baseline or threshold.
Evaluation methods for build success rates
The evaluation of build success rate effectiveness is mainly as follows:
• Evaluation based on baseline: After each build is completed, the success/failure status is
reported. The build success rate for a day is calculated, and after several days, a period of
stable daily build success rates is obtained. The average of these data provides the baseline
build success rate for that period. When the build success rate for a given day exceeds the
baseline by a significant amount (e.g., more than 20%), there may be a performance issue
in that build. Once the build success rate baseline is established, the current build success
rate can be compared to the baseline as an SLO; for example, it is considered healthy if it
is not lower than the baseline by more than 10%.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 212
• Evaluation based on thresholds: Set a fixed success rate threshold (e.g., 80%) according

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 211
chunks.content:
to business requirements, then conduct statistical analysis and comparison of all builds
within a fixed cycle. The cycle unit can be day, week, or month.
Once a build can be produced reliably, the next reliability concern is how changes are reviewed
and introduced into production. Change review helps SRE teams reduce release risk by identifying
architectural, operational, and non-functional issues before they affect users.
Change review
The main purpose of change review is to reduce risks brought by system changes going live
and to ensure changes are delivered to the business as scheduled. In change reviews, different
SRE organizations establish corresponding change review mechanisms at various stages of the
system delivery lifecycle, such as availability reviews at the project initiation stage, technical or
deployment architecture availability reviews, non-functional and operability reviews during the
design stage, and CAB reviews before going live.
Stability architecture design assessment
To promote stable architecture management, the SRE organization recommends establishing
a cross-team technical architecture management body at the technical level, responsible for
formulating stability architecture management specifications, technical component specifications,
and the corresponding technical management and review processes. SREs should focus on
advancing related assessment work in areas such as high availability, disaster recovery, scalability,
data integrity, and deployment environments.
High availability is a baseline requirement for operations management. The main task of operations
is to eliminate single points of failure and enhance system resilience. For example, in databases,
methods such as primary-standby, master-slave, and distributed architectures are used; in data
centers, active-active distribution in two sites and three centers or distributed multi-active setups
are utilized. Deploying a single application system with the same service component in multiple
data center rooms, on multiple virtual machines across different physical machines, providing
network hardware or software load balancers for application load balancing, and offering high-
availability architecture middleware such as PaaS cloud services are also approaches. To better
advance the assessment work, SREs need to provide high availability architecture specifications
in advance, develop reference models for high availability of general components and information
system architectures, and implement high availability requirements earlier in the system design
process.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 213
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 213
Disaster recovery can draw on best practices and the characteristics of specific information
systems to develop corresponding disaster recovery capability requirements. At the application
system layer, attention needs to be paid to application splitting, decoupling of service or
system interactions, stateless services, reducing dependencies on bus node services, increasing
asynchronous access mechanisms, multi-level caching, database optimization, rate limiting and
peak shaving mechanisms, foundational design for rapid scaling, etc. At the infrastructure layer, a
recoverable infrastructure environment should be able to effectively recover from natural or man-
made disasters, that is, considering various risks, including natural disasters, technical failures,
human errors, or network attacks, and taking preventive measures to reduce potential losses. At
a minimum, this should include backup, redundancy, rapid service recovery, and protection of
critical information systems.
The scalability of a technical architecture refers to the system’s ability to expand or enhance
its functionality without affecting existing system functions and performance. This usually
involves considerations about system design, architecture, and modularization to facilitate
future expansions and upgrades. Specifically, this includes: splitting the system into multiple
independent subsystems or modules, each responsible for specific functions and business
logic, reducing the complexity of the entire system and the coupling between modules, and
improving extensibility; supporting both horizontal and vertical scalability—by increasing
the number of servers and enhancing the processing capabilities of each server, the processing
power of the entire system can be improved, or by upgrading the hardware of a single server or
component, its processing power can be boosted; supporting elastic scaling, i.e., automatically
adjusting computing and storage resources based on the system load to achieve dynamic scaling
up and down; reducing dependencies on bus node services by changing logical interactions
composed of multiple nodes to end-to-end access methods, thereby reducing factors that affect
transactions; introducing asynchronous access mechanisms, as synchronous mechanisms may
exhaust maximum connections in a short time when performance issues occur—even if this
maximum concurrency is ten times that under normal circumstances—so switching synchronous
connections to asynchronous communication, or introducing message queues; supporting multi-
level caching, establishing caches at the frontend, within applications, at the database layer, etc.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 214
Data integrity is the baseline requirement for operations and maintenance assurance. The lifecycle

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 213
chunks.content:
of persistent data is usually much longer than the lifecycle of systems and hardware. When new
systems go online or architectural adjustments are made, data migration is often considered. At
the same time, attention must be paid to complex data processing such as batch, clearing, and
reconciliation operations, which are highly susceptible to data problems. The operations side
needs to focus on root cause analysis for abnormal interruptions in data processing, which
stages can be interrupted for emergency handling, whether multiple retries are supported after
interruption, and, in the event of data inconsistencies agreed upon with third-party systems,
which side should be used as the basis for emergency response mechanisms.
When selecting a deployment environment, multiple factors must be considered comprehensively,
such as application characteristics, performance requirements, scalability, reliability, security,
provider support, and cost-effectiveness. Different factors have important impacts on the
choice of deployment environment. For example, some applications may require large amounts
of memory and computing resources, some need platform services with high throughput and
robust data processing capabilities, others depend on cloud services to achieve scalability with
demand changes, and yet others need to choose infrastructure environments with high stability
and security.
Non-functional technical assessment
Non-functional design in operations and maintenance is the proactive entry point to address
maintainability issues, directly determining the cost and benefits of systems in the production
environment, and even the length of a system’s lifecycle. The following non-functional designs
need to be promoted by the operations side.
System operational observability
The three core elements of observability in cloud-native—monitoring metrics, logs, and tracing—
are equally applicable to traditional technical architectures represented by hosts. Operations and
maintenance (O&M) enhance these aspects on a finished black-box product, with solutions like
NPM, APM, and BPM initiated from the O&M side. From a non-functional design perspective,
improving observability requires shifting O&M involvement forward, promoting necessary R&D
standards for monitoring, logs, and tracing, improving the ability to proactively report monitoring
performance metric data, optimizing log readability, and providing essential infrastructure
services support, such as supporting system monitoring data reporting, log collection and analysis.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 215
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 215
Fault isolation and service degradation
The purpose of fault isolation and service degradation is to sacrifice part of business functionality
or part of customers’ business to ensure the service quality of more critical businesses or customer
groups. This approach prevents cascading failures. In design, the O&M side needs to review all
the service components called by the application system from a system or business perspective
and plan assumptions and countermeasures for faults in each service component.
Performance evaluation
Performance and capacity management are mainly based on golden metrics such as response
time (the time a system, function, or service component takes to complete handling an external
request), throughput (the maximum number of requests that can be handled within a specified
time), load (the current load status of the service component), efficiency (performance divided
by resources, such as QPS = concurrency/average response time), and scalability (the ability
for vertical or horizontal expansion). Performance issues challenge stability not just through a
single component’s unavailability but more significantly when a component’s performance issues
spread to others, causing large-scale failures. Performance problems are highly likely to trigger
complex exceptions, so SREs need to conduct strengthened technical evaluations accordingly.
Backward compatibility of mobile terminal versions
The management of mobile terminal versions is becoming increasingly important. In architecture
design, on one hand, it is necessary to ensure that upgraded versions are as backward compatible
as possible with lower versions still in circulation; on the other hand, convergence management
of existing versions should be performed, supporting a variety of online update mechanisms.
Running based on the fundamental platform
Whether dealing with infrastructure platforms, PaaS-level application platforms, or continuous
delivery toolchains, the system should integrate with the company’s existing fundamental
platforms whenever possible, avoiding the introduction of new technology stacks, and should be
implemented in a configurable manner to avoid hardcoding. In emergency situations, the author
has found that some parameters were hardcoded in the program, preventing rapid adjustments;
thus, configuration management needs to be strengthened. Converting IPs to DNS domain names
is also a direction for configuration, aimed at reducing manual backend modifications.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 216
Log standardization
Log analysis is an important means to understand application systems. SREs should focus on the
following aspects: First is storage. Due to industry or internal enterprise requirements for log
data retention, there needs to be a cost-controllable, horizontally scalable platform that supports

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 215
chunks.content:
massive log data management; Second is querying. Logs are an important window for perceiving
the operational state of online systems and locating code-level problems. In scenarios such as
business issues and emergency incidents, problems can be identified through log queries. Therefore,
it is necessary to establish real-time data collection and efficient log retrieval capabilities;
Third is monitoring, which provides monitoring capabilities through keyword analysis, regex
searches, and pattern matching of logs; Fourth is analysis, where the unstructured data in logs
is processed into structured data to support running data analysis, achieving anomaly detection,
fault localization, performance analysis, and capacity evaluation functions.
Comprehensive test plans
During test plan reviews, SREs should focus on reviewing plans for performance, capacity, stress,
and stability architecture tests. The review perspectives include whether the description of test
cases is clear, whether the execution results of test cases meet requirements, and whether the
test conclusions address countermeasures for legacy issues, etc.
While change review focuses on whether a change is technically and operationally acceptable,
change protection preparation focuses on whether the organization is ready to respond if the
change causes instability. This includes monitoring, emergency plans, documentation, and
knowledge-base readiness.
Change protection preparation assessment
Changes can pose stability risks to the system. Judging from the rate of failures caused by
production changes, incidents triggered by changes are far higher than those from other factors.
After a change, it is usually the busiest period for operations organizations. Whether it is a large
software baseline, a functional iteration, or even a parameter or configuration adjustment, any
of these can cause major failures. There are many risk points in changes, including program
defects in design, version control issues in management, operational execution problems, and
even interdependent impacts caused by poor communication between upstream and downstream
systems at the collaboration level. Solving the risks brought by changes is a highly complex and
systematic task. SREs should consider strengthening the evaluation of change protection from
the following aspects.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 217
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 217
Are monitoring and alerting ready?
Comprehensive monitoring coverage includes technical indicators such as infrastructure, platform
software, databases, middleware, operating systems, and performance, as well as business
function and customer experience indicators relevant to specific systems.
Establishing a complete monitoring and alerting system is an important way to ensure system
maintainability. It allows for real-time monitoring of various system metrics, timely identification
of problems, proactive alerting, and rapid resolution of issues.
Are emergency plans ready?
First, are fault emergency tools ready? When a system failure occurs, it is necessary to restore and
resolve the issue quickly to prevent the fault from escalating. Second, is the technical operation
work in place? After the system goes live, comprehensive operational management is required,
including user service, tracking the first business transaction, handling abnormal data or logic
problems, security management, etc., to ensure stable and efficient system operation.
Are the documents complete?
According to the organization’s software delivery collaboration mechanism, clarify the
documentation delivery checklist for the launch of the new system, such as project, and
requirements, technical architecture diagrams, test conclusions (including stress testing),
installation and deployment (environment-related), application/business monitoring, initial
transaction function monitoring and assurance, list of key functions, important configurations,
and parameters, operational performance evaluation, etc.
Is the knowledge base ready?
Establishing a comprehensive knowledge base is an important foundation to ensure the
maintainability of the system. Provide detailed descriptions of various functions and operations
of the system, and build a knowledge base to facilitate quick retrieval of relevant information
when needed.
New systems and new business launches require broader assurance than routine changes because
they introduce new architecture, new user behavior, new business dependencies, and new
operational uncertainty. For this reason, SRE teams must assess both technical readiness and
business-impact risk before go-live.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 218
New system or new business go-live assurance assessment
The rollout of a new system or new business is a process from zero to one, and the specific
work usually includes go-live preparation, technical solution formulation, evaluation and test
management, preparation of go-live documentation, risk assessment, security assurance measures,
operations monitoring preparation, go-live process coordination, release, system acceptance, and
go-live trial operation, etc.
The go-live of a new system or new business brings both opportunities and challenges to an

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 217
chunks.content:
enterprise: on the one hand, as an important project milestone, the new system will empower
the enterprise’s business development or operations management. Usually, the business demand
side will invest a lot of effort in the post-launch operational promotion work, in hopes of better
bringing value to the business and customers; on the other hand, launching a new system brings
numerous uncertainties that need to be managed.
Risk assessment work for SREs
In risk assessment work, the SRE should strengthen the evaluation of the following risks:
• Risks brought by new business, regulatory compliance, data security, privacy protection,
etc.
• Risks to the new system’s business process availability, endpoint experience, and data
accuracy
• The impact of the new business system on the capacity and performance of existing
upstream and downstream systems, as well as the effect of upstream and downstream
integration or transformation on the original business
• Whether the resources, architecture, and key functions of the new system meet business
expectations, and whether they satisfy the performance and capacity requirements of
upcoming business activities
• Whether system stress tests, capacity evaluation plans, unresolved functional defects,
etc., have been adequately assessed
After identifying the risks that SRE teams need to assess before a new system or business launch,
the next step is to define the proactive actions they can take to reduce those risks and improve
go-live readiness.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 219
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 219
Proactive actions for SRE
In addition, the SRE should proactively promote the following work:
• Start with standardization, establish compliance, risk, privacy, and security management
requirements at both business and technical levels, and assist with relevant technical
detection tools
• Build non-functional requirements for business systems, such as system rollback,
version switching, canary releases, endpoint experience perception, and other support
functionalities
• Build technical operations requirements for business systems, such as initial business
perception, business transaction monitoring, and technical operations monitoring of
related systems
System performance and capacity management, such as related evaluation metrics, baseline
capacity design, metric data processing, capacity assessment analysis reports, and construction
of tools like stress testing.
At the same time, in response to potential surges in business patterns, the SRE needs to establish
rate limiting and traffic shaping mechanisms. In terms of architecture optimization, the front-
end system should set up trading concurrency control switches, and implement front-end rate
limiting and traffic shaping as needed, as well as back-end service degradation. Through front-
end interaction design, reduce the impact on customer experience, with a key focus on ensuring
the stability of the system’s core services.
SRE focuses on the launch phase of new systems or new services, shifting operations and
maintenance work to the left, building up resource delivery capabilities in advance to improve
system go-live speed, leveraging operation and maintenance platform capabilities to assist in
the development of business logic, and participating early in the development and acceptance

With the rapid development of IT services, effective analysis and management of massive data

and machine translation, and LLMs have achieved significant progress in various NLP downstream
tasks. Against this backdrop, Operations and Maintenance (O&M) scenarios need to actively

incorporate LLMs to enhance traditional automated O&M capabilities, accelerate entry into the

Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 224
Improving log O&M with LLMs
Logs are an important and widely existing data modality in the field of O&M. However, for O&M
teams, accurately processing and analyzing logs has always been an extremely difficult problem.
As a result, in daily O&M management, logs are hard to utilize efficiently and lose their inherent
value. With the development of LLMs, this situation has improved. In O&M scenarios, personnel
benefit from the powerful semantic understanding capabilities of LLMs, making many previously
challenging log processing and analysis tasks much simpler. For example, by leveraging the
contextual learning abilities of LLMs, O&M staff can achieve highly accurate, automated, end-to-
end generation of business code log instrumentation. At the same time, highly efficient parameter
fine-tuning techniques of LLMs have also addressed issues in log parsing.
Meanwhile, as one of the three main pillars of observability data, logs contain important system
information and play a key role in O&M management and business continuity assurance. Based
on log information, potential system or network issues can be quickly identified, reducing system
downtime and improving service availability. Additionally, logs help identify security threats,
such as intrusions and fraud, which are crucial for ensuring information security.
Recognizing challenges in log monitoring
Some major issues include: processing massive volumes of log data in real-time scenarios; the lack
of unified standards for log formats—logs generated by different applications and devices may
differ greatly in structure and content; logs may contain large amounts of normal or irrelevant
information, making it harder to identify true anomalies. The constant evolution of system and
network environments also leads to ever-changing anomaly patterns, requiring detection methods
to be highly adaptable.
In intelligent log O&M scenarios, traditional log analysis faces many technical difficulties.
Ultimately, it is necessary to apply LLM technologies to enhance applications in log analysis in
order to better support business continuity.
To understand how LLMs can improve log operations and maintenance, it is useful to first review
