chunks.content:
what logs capture and how they support daily O&M work.
Concept of logs
Logs are important tools in information technology and network management for recording and
tracking the operational status of systems, networks, and applications. These logs are crucial for
system administrators, O&M management personnel, and information security management
staff.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 225
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 225
They provide detailed information needed for diagnosing problems, monitoring system
performance, and ensuring system security. The main types of operational and maintenance
logs are as follows:
• System Logs: Record the activities of the operating system, such as system startup and
shutdown, system errors, hardware failures, and other system-level events
• Application Logs: Record the operation history of applications, such as application startup
and shutdown, operations performed by the application, internal errors, user activities,
and more
• Security Logs: Record all security-related events, such as login attempts (successful or
failed), permission changes, firewall alerts, network intrusion attempts, and more
• Network Logs: Record the status of network devices, such as operational data of routers,
switches, load balancers, as well as network traffic and abnormal traffic activities, etc.
After understanding the main types of logs used in O&M, it is useful to look at how these logs move
through the operational workflow. In practice, log O&M usually follows a process of collecting log
data, analyzing it for signals or anomalies, and responding to the issues revealed by that analysis.
Basic process of log O&M
The basic process of log O&M includes log collection, log analysis, and log response, as shown
in Figure 7.1.
Figure 7.1: Basic process of log O&M
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 226
(1) Log collection
Log collection is the first step in log O&M management. It involves collecting log data from
various information systems, applications, devices, etc. The collected logs include system logs,
application logs, security logs, network logs, and so on. The key to the log collection process is to
use automated tools to continuously collect data while also ensuring the integrity and timeliness
of the log data.
Operations personnel transmit log data to log management systems or data storage media for
centralized storage as needed. In the process of dealing with log collection and log management,
there are a variety of platforms and tools to choose from, each with its own characteristics and
advantages. The combination of Elasticsearch, Logstash, and Kibana is a very popular open-
source log management solution. Elasticsearch is used for data storage and search, Logstash for
log collection and processing, and Kibana for data visualization and analysis. In addition, there
are also tools such as Splunk and Graylog. Splunk is also a powerful commercial solution that
provides functions for log collection, monitoring, searching, analysis, and visualization. It is
suitable for large-scale log management environments and supports real-time data processing
and complex analytical queries. Graylog is an open-source log management platform that offers

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 225
chunks.content:
rich features for log collection, storage, querying, and reporting, and is known for its ease of use
and robust log processing capabilities. Each of these platforms and tools has its own strengths.
When choosing the right log collection platform, it is necessary to decide based on specific business
needs, budget, and technical environment. Generally, Elasticsearch and Graylog have advantages
in cost control, while Splunk is more comprehensive in functionality and support services.
(2) Log analysis
After logs are collected and stored, the next step is to analyze these logs to identify patterns,
trends, and potential issues. The principle of log analysis is based on data mining and statistical
techniques, providing insights by identifying patterns, trends, and abnormal behaviors in logs. For
example, by analyzing failed login log entries, it may be possible to identify unauthorized access
in the system; by monitoring system performance logs, resource usage peaks can be detected and
future system bottlenecks may be predicted. In practice, artificial intelligence technology can be
applied to log analysis. For instance, machine learning techniques can automatically learn log
patterns and sound alerts when behaviors deviate from the expected patterns. Such analysis
is not limited to detecting known problems but can also predict and prevent upcoming issues
through continuous learning.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 227
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 227
Overall, log analysis is a complex but crucial process that plays an irreplaceable role in maintaining
system stability and security. At the same time, an effective log analysis strategy can greatly
enhance the efficiency and responsiveness of operational and maintenance organizations.
(3) Log response
Log response is the final stage in the log management process. Its main goal is to take appropriate
action based on the results of log analysis, to resolve issues, optimize system performance, or
enhance security. Effective log response not only helps resolve technical problems in a timely
manner, but also prevents potential security threats and ensures the continuous and stable
operation of the system. The main steps of log response are as follows:
1. Alert Generation: Based on analysis results, when abnormal activities or performance
metrics exceeding preset thresholds are detected, the log system automatically generates
alerts. Alerts are the trigger point of the response process. Their design should avoid being
overly sensitive, to reduce false positives, and at the same time not be too sluggish, so as
to avoid missing critical events.
2. Problem Diagnosis: Upon receiving an alert, the operations team needs to further analyze
the relevant log data to diagnose the root cause of the problem. This may include reviewing
detailed logs from specific time periods, performance indicators of related systems, and
interactions with other systems or applications.
3. Action Execution: After diagnosis is complete, the operations team will take appropriate
measures depending on the nature of the issue, which may include restarting services,
adjusting configurations, updating software or hardware, or optimizing resource allocation,
etc.
4. Feedback Loop: Lessons learned during the log response process should be fed back
into log management and operations processes, serving as the basis for adjusting and
optimizing alert settings, analysis procedures, and response strategies
The principle of log response is to quickly and accurately translate log analysis into concrete actions,
handling system issues with minimal delay. Effective log response relies on highly automated
tools and processes to ensure an immediate response when issues are detected. Automation
plays a central role in log response, from automatically triggering alerts to executing predefined
response measures, which can greatly increase handling speed and reduce human errors. In
addition, advanced analytical techniques such as machine learning can further optimize the
response process, enabling predictive maintenance to prevent problems before they occur, rather
than merely solving existing issues.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 228
In summary, log response is a dynamic, multi-layered process involving rapid transition from data

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 227
chunks.content:
analysis to concrete action, and its effectiveness is directly related to organizational operational
efficiency and system stability. Through continuous optimization and technological advancement,
log response can become a powerful tool in enterprise information system management.
Although this collection-analysis-response workflow is well established, it becomes difficult
to manage at scale because logs are large, distributed, inconsistent, and often hard to interpret.
Addressing log O&M pain points with LLMs
Although logs are essential for monitoring system health and diagnosing incidents, their value
depends on whether O&M teams can locate the right information, understand what it means,
and decide how to respond. In daily operations, these three steps often become the main sources
of difficulty.
O&M personnel cannot find abnormal logs
When managing and monitoring IT infrastructure, it is crucial for O&M personnel to discover
and identify abnormal logs. However, they often face the challenge of being unable to locate
abnormal logs, which can be caused by various factors, mainly including the following aspects.
The volume of log data is too large. When log capacity reaches the TB or even PB level, it not
only imposes higher requirements on the log storage system but also significantly increases the
complexity of data management, making it extremely difficult for O&M personnel to find valuable
information within this massive amount of data—like looking for a needle in a haystack.
Tools by capability
LLM-assisted log operations usually build on existing observability and log-manage -
ment pipelines rather than replacing them. Common tools for log collection, storage,
search, and analysis include Elastic Stack or OpenSearch, Splunk, Grafana Loki, Data -
dog, and Sumo Logic. OpenTelemetry is also becoming an important vendor-neutral
standard for collecting logs, metrics, and traces across distributed systems.
In practice, these tools provide the operational data pipeline, while LLMs can be
added to help summarize logs, identify abnormal patterns, explain key messages,
correlate logs with other context, and recommend troubleshooting steps.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 229
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 229
Log sources are dispersed. In large distributed systems, logs may be scattered across multiple
different servers, devices, and applications. The lack of a unified log collection and management
system leads to scattered logs, making it difficult for O&M personnel to access all relevant logs
from a central point.
Lack of log standardization. In environments without a unified log format and standards, O&M
personnel may find it hard to understand and analyze log data coming from different systems.
Improper log configuration could result in key information not being recorded. For example, if
the log level is set too high, some alerts or error information might not be logged; conversely, it
might generate a large amount of redundant information, obscuring important alerts.
O&M personnel cannot understand key logs
O&M personnel may encounter difficulties understanding key logs, mainly due to the following
two reasons.
The technical nature of log files themselves. Because log files often contain highly technical
information and professional jargon, lacking relevant knowledge will directly affect the
understanding of log content. In addition, as technology updates and iterates, new systems and
applications may introduce unfamiliar log formats or new error codes. If O&M personnel fail to
update their knowledge base in time, it will also affect their understanding of logs.
Complex log formats lead to poor readability. In diversified IT environments, different systems,
devices, and applications may generate log files in different formats. If these log files lack a unified
format or do not follow industry standards, it greatly increases the difficulty for O&M personnel
to interpret logs. Inconsistent log formats mean that O&M staff need to master more parsing
skills and invest more time and effort in understanding a variety of log structures and content.
O&M personnel do not know what to do when facing log
messages
When facing massive log data, O&M personnel often feel confused, and the reasons can be
analyzed from the following three aspects:
• Lack of clear response procedures or guidance: O&M personnel often find it difficult
to determine what actions to take, the order of priorities, and who to contact during
the problem-solving process when faced with specific log events, due to the absence of
predefined response procedures or standard operating procedures. This uncertainty
not only delays issue resolution time but may also lead to improper handling of issues.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 230
• Insufficient automation and tool support: In many cases, O&M staff may not have
adequate tool support to help them effectively analyze and respond to information in
logs. The lack of automation tools means that personnel must manually sift through

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 229
chunks.content:
and analyze massive amounts of log data, which is not only inefficient but also prone to
errors. Furthermore, if the existing tools cannot provide sufficient analytical depth or are
not user-friendly, the difficulty for O&M personnel increases when dealing with complex
or voluminous logs.
• Insufficient expertise and experience: O&M personnel may lack the specialized
knowledge or experience to handle specific types of logs. This situation is common in
rapidly evolving IT environments, where logs generated by new technologies or systems
may contain new information or error codes that they have not encountered before. If
O&M staff do not have an adequate understanding of these new elements, even if they
can read the log data, they may not know how to effectively diagnose and resolve issues
based on the log contents.
These pain points show why LLMs are useful in log O&M: they can help detect abnormal patterns,
interpret complex log messages, and recommend next steps for incident response.
How to address log O&M pain points
The log O&M pain points discussed earlier can be addressed in three connected ways. First,
models can help detect abnormal log patterns that are difficult for O&M personnel to find
manually. Second, LLMs can help interpret key logs by combining log content with system
knowledge, documentation, source code, or enterprise context. Third, LLM-powered workflows
can recommend response actions, support fault localization, and guide O&M personnel through
standard operating procedures.
Detecting abnormal logs with LLM-assisted analysis
In modern IT infrastructure management, machine learning algorithms are widely used to improve
the efficiency and accuracy of log analysis, especially in automatically discovering anomalous
logs. Machine learning can help O&M personnel automatically identify abnormal patterns in
the system, so as to respond to and deal with potential issues in a timely manner. The following
are several key steps for using machine learning algorithms to solve the problem of anomalous
logs being difficult to detect.

(1) Data preprocessing
Before using machine learning algorithms, log data needs to be preprocessed. The steps include
data cleaning (removing irrelevant data, correcting erroneous data), normalization (unifying
log formats), feature extraction (extracting meaningful information from logs as input to the
model), etc. Effective data preprocessing can greatly improve the efficiency of model training
and prediction accuracy.
(2) Feature engineering
Feature engineering is a vital part of machine learning, involving the selection, modification, and
creation of new features to enhance model performance. In log analysis, common features include
the timestamp of log entries, source IP addresses, error codes, operation codes, etc. Advanced
features include keywords or phrases extracted from log text or statistical information based on
the event frequency within a time window.
(3) Selecting appropriate machine learning models
Selecting suitable machine learning models according to the characteristics of the log data and
business needs is essential. For anomaly detection, commonly used algorithms include clustering
algorithms, distance-based anomaly detection, and neural networks.
Typical clustering algorithms include K-means and DBSCAN. These unsupervised learning
algorithms can help identify natural groups in the data, with outliers usually not belonging to
any main group. In distance-based anomaly detection, typical examples are the Isolation Forest
algorithm and the LOF (Local Outlier Factor) algorithm, which identify anomalies by considering
the distance between data points and their neighbors. Among neural networks, autoencoders are
a typical example, mainly suitable for handling large-scale data sets and complex data structures.
They can learn the normal patterns of data and identify anomalous data that deviate from these
patterns.
In 2024, at the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, a paper by Yunzhihui titled LOGFORMER: A
Pre-train and Tuning Pipeline for Log Anomaly Detection elaborated on how to use machine learning
techniques for log anomaly detection. According to the paper, Yunzhihui based their approach on
the Transformer model and used adapter fine-tuning to solve the semantic information sharing
issue between different log sources. Log anomaly detection is a key component in the field of
intelligent O&M. In real industrial scenarios, logs from different sources can vary significantly.
Early anomaly detection models only focused on extracting semantics from the log sequences of
the same source, resulting in poor generalization to logs from multiple different sources. Retraining
detection models with data from unknown log sources is inefficient.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 232
Although there are morphological and syntactic differences among different log sources, they

often share the same semantic space. As shown in Figure 7.2, if there are similar anomalies from
multiple domains, the top shows “Abnormal Program Termination” anomaly analysis for the
domains BGL, Thunderbird, and Red Storm, while the bottom shows “Program Not Running”
anomaly analysis for the domains BGL, Thunderbird, Spirit, and Liberty.
Figure 7.2: Case of similarity anomaly
To address this problem, one example approach, proposed by Yunzhihui, is a unified Transformer-
based log anomaly detection framework called LogFormer, aimed at improving the generalization
capability across different log domains. This framework comprises a pre-training phase and an
adapter-based fine-tuning phase. Specifically, the log anomaly detection framework first performs
pre-training on the source domain to acquire shared semantic knowledge from log data, and
then transfers this knowledge to the target domain via shared parameters. In addition, the model
introduces a Log Attention module to supplement information that is overlooked during log
pattern parsing. Results from multiple benchmark experiments demonstrate that LogFormer
is effective while utilizing fewer trainable parameters and incurring lower training costs. The
structure of the LogFormer framework is shown in Figure 7.3: first, the log sequences are input
to the pre-trained language model to extract features; the Log-Attention encoder is then trained
on the source domain to obtain shared semantic information; finally, the encoder is initialized,
and knowledge transfer to the target domain is accomplished by adjusting the target domain
adapter ’s parameters.

These steps describe the general machine learning pipeline for anomaly detection. Recent
Transformer-based approaches build on this foundation by learning shared semantic patterns
across log sources, making anomaly detection more adaptable in environments where logs come
from different systems and formats.
Understanding the LogFormer workflow
LogFormer addresses the above issues in two working phases: the Log Attention Encoding Phase
and the Cross-domain Adapter Fine-tuning Phase.
Preserving log semantics with Log Attention
The Log Attention Encoding Phase preserves semantic knowledge shared between different
domains. Specifically, to avoid information loss caused by log pattern parsing, the Log Attention
module models log sequences and makes additional use of parameter information that is neglected
in log pattern parsing, thereby achieving better performance. Compared to traditional structures,
the model additionally incorporates parameter information lost during log pattern parsing. The
LogFormer model structure is depicted in Figure 7.4, with the left part showing multi-head
encoding and the right part showing parameter encoding.

Evaluating the effect of pre-training and adapter fine-tuning
In addition to the main experimental results, Yunzhihui also conducted data ablation experiments.
To verify the effectiveness of pre-training, the performance of LogFormer-s and LogFormer-p
was compared at the data level. Yunzhihui chose BGL as the pre-training log source due to the
diversity of its log templates, and compared the two strategies— pre-training and training from
scratch —in terms of loss and F1 scores. Figure 7.8 shows the loss and F1 score curves during
the training process. The results indicate that fine-tuning after pre-training converges faster
than training from scratch, demonstrating that knowledge learned from the source domain is
of significant value.
Figure 7.8: Loss and F1 score curves
Experiments have proven that pre-training can accelerate convergence without sacrificing
performance, but fine-tuning is usually costly and important. Therefore, in the experiments,
Yunzhihui adopted adapter-based fine-tuning, which adds extra trainable parameters to obtain
a compact model for log anomaly detection. To verify the effectiveness of adapter-based fine-
tuning, LogFormer-p was compared with LogFormer on the HDFS and Thunderbird datasets.
As shown in Figure 7.9, the F1 value generated by LogFormer (with an average increase of 1%) is
slightly higher than direct fine-tuning of the pre-trained model on both datasets. In addition,
adapter-based fine-tuning used only 3.5% to 5.5% of trainable parameters, requiring very few
parameter adjustments.

According to the experimental results, LogFormer is a pre-training and fine-tuning process flow
for log anomaly detection, which includes a pre-training phase and an adapter-based fine-tuning
phase. To better encode log sequence information, Yunzhihui proposed a log attention module
processing method. Experiments also showed that LogFormer has fewer trainable parameters
and lower training costs, and its performance surpasses most baseline models.
Detecting abnormal logs is only the first step. After an anomaly is found, O&M personnel still
need to understand what the log means, which system or component it relates to, and what
contextual information is needed to interpret it correctly.
Interpreting key logs with LLMs and RAG
To address the issue that O&M personnel cannot understand logs, logs must first be classified.
Typically, logs can be divided into three types: common open-source logs, enterprise internal
system logs, and specialized domain logs.
First of all, for open-source logs, LLMs already has good analysis capabilities, and using model fine-
tuning (SFT) technology can slightly improve the parsing capability for open-source component

logs. However, as base models are updated and iterated, the improvement is often less than that
brought by the new generation of base models. Therefore, the evaluation of open-source LLMs
has become particularly important.
Secondly, enterprise internal system logs need to be addressed with the assistance of RAG
technology. Typically, for log data within an enterprise’s private domain, the internal information
system needs to provide related internal information, including structured data and source code
data, etc. This type of information is usually referred to as Feed. The interaction process between
Feed and LLMs is shown in Figure 7.10, which can realize error analysis of log call stacks and locate
source code, with the LLM ultimately providing an analysis result.

LLMs.
Guiding O&M responses with LLMs
Faced with complex log data, operations personnel often feel at a loss, especially when trying
to quickly pinpoint the source of faults, execute standard operating procedures, and provide
feedback on log analysis results. The application of LLMs can help operations personnel better
solve the following problems.
Solving the problem of rapid fault localization
When a fault is discovered and needs to be located through logs, quickly identifying the problem
and finding the responsible person for handling it is a key step. Usually, system emergency plans
need to provide a clear list of responsible personnel and information delivery avenues, clearly
defining responsible persons for various common faults and integrating this information into the
log management system. For example, operations personnel can configure automatic notification
mechanisms for each type of error or alert to ensure that relevant technical staff quickly receive
fault information. Operations personnel can also use intelligent troubleshooting tools, such
as fault diagnosis systems based on LLMs, which can analyze log data, automatically infer the
severity level of issues, and assign them to the appropriate team or individual according to rules.
Providing standard operating procedures and recommendations for
operations personnel
The use of standard operating procedures and automation tools can greatly improve the efficiency
of operations personnel in handling logs and faults. Developing and refining standard operating
procedures for operations is a good approach; typically, operations personnel need to formulate
detailed SOPs for various common log-indicated issues. These manuals should include step-by-
step instructions, required tools, precautions, etc., ensuring that even inexperienced operations
personnel can resolve problems step-by-step. Implement automated response tools, deploying
automation scripts and tools (such as Ansible, Chef, or Puppet) to automatically handle common

log events and faults. For instance, services can be automatically restarted, disk space can be
cleaned up, or systems can be rolled back to the most recent stable state.

Improving the feedback mechanism of the log platform
An effective feedback mechanism ensures that the log platform continuously improves and better
serves operational and maintenance needs. Firstly, regarding the integration of feedback channels,
operations personnel integrate feedback channels into the log analysis platform, allowing users
to quickly report issues, make improvement suggestions, or request assistance. Secondly, regular
review and updates are essential. Operations personnel regularly review collected feedback,
analyze the usage and user satisfaction of the log platform, and periodically update log processing
logic, user interfaces, and features based on this information to ensure the platform can adapt to
ever-changing IT environments and user needs.

Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 242
After examining how LLMs can help O&M teams detect, interpret, and respond to log events, the
next step is to look at how operational knowledge can be organized and reused. An intelligent
O&M knowledge base gives teams a structured way to store troubleshooting guides, system
documentation, historical cases, and domain knowledge, while LLMs make that knowledge easier
to search, summarize, and apply during daily operations.
Building an intelligent O&M knowledge base
This is an instance of the Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pattern, applied to the O&M
knowledge-base domain. A knowledge base is a system or database in which an organization or
institution centrally stores and manages knowledge and information. It is a structured knowledge
management tool used to collect, organize, store, and share various types of knowledge, such as
documents, manuals, guides, and case studies. The aim of a knowledge base is to help people easily
access and share knowledge, improve work efficiency, and enhance problem-solving capabilities.
Difficulties and advantages of building an O&M knowledge
base
Building a traditional knowledge base involves the following steps:
1. Determining the scope and objectives of the knowledge base
2. Collecting and organizing knowledge materials
3. Structuring and classifying knowledge
4. Selecting appropriate knowledge base tools and platforms
5. Designing user interfaces and search functions
Tools by capability
An intelligent O&M knowledge base typically combines document storage, retrieval,

trieval components include Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Faiss, and pgvector. Lang -
Chain and LlamaIndex are widely used orchestration frameworks for connecting
documents, embeddings, vector stores, retrieval logic, prompts, and LLMs into RAG
workflows.
These tools provide the technical foundation for turning O&M documents, trouble -
shooting guides, FAQs, runbooks, and historical incident records into searchable
knowledge that an LLM can use when answering operational questions.

6. Establishing a knowledge base maintenance mechanism
7. Iterating and continuously improving the knowledge base
In an O&M context, these steps need to account for the specific kinds of operational knowledge
that teams use during troubleshooting, deployment, monitoring, and recovery.
In the O&M field, an O&M knowledge base generally contains various types of information
related to system operation, management, and maintenance. For example, system architecture
and topology diagrams, configuration documents, operating manuals, troubleshooting
guides, backup and recovery strategies, performance optimization recommendations, update
and maintenance logs, FAQs, etc. This information can help O&M teams understand system
architecture, configuration, and operational status, as well as guide them in handling common
issues and failures.
Challenges in building an O&M knowledge base
Although these knowledge sources are valuable, turning them into a usable and maintainable
knowledge base presents several practical challenges:
• Knowledge Organization and Classification: Organizing and classifying vast amounts
of knowledge is a complex task, requiring the establishment of reasonable classification
standards and systems so that users can easily obtain the required knowledge.
• Knowledge Updating and Maintenance: A knowledge base needs regular updating and
maintenance, including adding new knowledge, updating existing knowledge, deleting
outdated knowledge, etc., and establishing effective mechanisms to ensure the timeliness
and quality of knowledge.
• User Experience and Search Effectiveness: Designing user-friendly interfaces and search
functions is key. User habits and needs must be considered, providing convenient search
and navigation capabilities to ensure that users can quickly find the knowledge they need.
• Knowledge Protection and Security: For certain sensitive or internal knowledge,
knowledge protection and security issues must be fully considered. Proper permission
management and access control mechanisms should be established to ensure the security
and confidentiality of knowledge.
These challenges explain why LLMs are useful in O&M knowledge-base scenarios: they can help
organize, retrieve, summarize, and apply operational knowledge more effectively than keyword-
based systems alone.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 244
Advantages of combining O&M knowledge bases with LLMs
By combining the O&M knowledge base with LLMs, one can leverage powerful language
understanding and generation capabilities obtained from training on massive textual data. This
is mainly used for automatic question answering, text summarization, semantic analysis, and
other tasks. Therefore, compared with traditional O&M knowledge bases, the combination of

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops

LLMs and knowledge bases offers the following advantages:
• Automated Knowledge Extraction and Classification: LLMs can automatically extract
and retrieve knowledge by training on vast amounts of textual data. They can recognize
entities, relationships, and concepts within text, helping to build the classification
structures and labels of knowledge bases.
• Automated Question Answering and Problem Solving: Based on the language
understanding and generation abilities of LLMs, they can be used to automatically answer
user queries and provide direct knowledge lookup and solutions. In O&M knowledge bases,
this can be used for quickly locating and retrieving specific knowledge points.
• Text Summarization and Knowledge Distillation: LLMs can automatically perform
text summarization and knowledge distillation, extracting key information and main
viewpoints from large amounts of text to help O&M personnel quickly understand and
acquire knowledge.
• Clustering and Association Analysis: LLMs can cluster texts and perform association
analysis to identify similarities and connections between texts. This can be used for related
recommendations and knowledge association analysis in knowledge bases, helping O&M
personnel discover more relevant knowledge.
• Knowledge Enhancement and Supplementation: Knowledge bases can be enhanced
and supplemented by integrating LLMs. Through interaction with these models, the
knowledge generated by models can be combined with manually curated knowledge,
improving the coverage and quality of the O&M knowledge base. To support these
capabilities, an O&M knowledge base needs broad coverage across both technical domains
and common operational tasks.
Many leading enterprises, during the process of building O&M knowledge bases, have
accumulated vast and high-quality O&M datasets, covering many common areas in the

• Information security

Once the purpose, content, and advantages of an LLM-enhanced O&M knowledge base are clear,
the next step is to examine how such a system can be built in practice.
Technical pathway for building an operations knowledge
base
Building an intelligent O&M knowledge base requires more than collecting documents in one place.
The system needs a clear construction plan, a way to process and structure different document
types, and a retrieval workflow that allows LLMs to use the right operational knowledge when
answering user questions. The following steps show how these parts fit together in practice.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 246
Overall construction plan for the operations knowledge base
The construction plan for the operations knowledge base includes the following four steps, as
shown in Figure 7.13.
Figure 7.13: Overall construction plan for the operations knowledge base
1. Requirements Analysis: Clarify the objectives, scope, and target audience of the knowledge
base
2. Data Collection: Collect and organize both internal and external company documents,
including data from various sources
3. Formulate the Operations Knowledge Base Plan: Conduct data preprocessing, split
and store documents so that LLMs can better understand document information; deploy
LLMs and coordinate scheduling of computing resources to fully utilize existing resources
4. Iteration and Update of the Knowledge Base: Regularly evaluate and optimize the
operations knowledge base
Among these steps, document preprocessing and structuring are especially important because
they determine how effectively the knowledge base can retrieve relevant information and how
accurately the LLM can use that information to answer O&M questions. The next subsection
focuses on this part of the workflow in more detail.
Document structuring and decomposition algorithms
When building an operations knowledge base, most data exist in the form of documents. Common
document formats include docx, pdf, txt, csv, etc. These document data come in various styles
and have varying quality. How to handle these documents is critical to ensuring effective Q&A
performance of the knowledge base. Therefore, it is necessary to use document structuring

information within the documents.

such as reports and tutorials, and helps improve the effectiveness of text vectorization. When
building the operations knowledge base and facing massive amounts of knowledge, the
document structuring and decomposition algorithm needs to consider the overall context and
the relationships among sentences and phrases within the text, resulting in more comprehensive

At the same time, many enterprises have found in practice that they usually already have their
own knowledge base systems in place (such as Wiki, Confluence, etc.). These knowledge bases
have accumulated a large amount of internal knowledge over years of development. Due to user
habits, data security, and other factors, enterprises are often reluctant to migrate their existing
knowledge bases. To address this, LLMs support interfacing with these internal knowledge bases
and decomposing the related structured documents. The specific process is shown in Figure 7.15.

A complete operations knowledge base construction process includes three main workflows:
knowledge base construction process, knowledge base Q&A process, and interfacing with
existing knowledge bases process.
Figure 7.15: Decomposition process of structured documents
These workflows show how documents are ingested, how user questions are answered, and how
existing enterprise knowledge bases can be connected without requiring a full migration.
In the knowledge base construction phase, a structured splitting algorithm is used to segment
and store various documents uploaded by users (such as docx, pdf, txt, etc.), and an embedding
lightweight model is used to vectorize the split document fragments, after which the information
is stored in a vector database.
During the knowledge base Q&A phase, the user’s input question is first processed with Query
Enhancement. A LLM is used to enrich and enhance the user’s question in order to retrieve
more relevant document fragments. Based on the structured splitting algorithm, the contextual
information of the relevant document fragments is located. After obtaining sufficient document
fragments, a reranking model selects and orders the fragments, filtering out some irrelevant
information. The resulting document fragments are then concatenated with Q&A prompts from
the knowledge base and passed to a LLM to generate the final answer, which is returned to the user.

After the construction workflow is established, the value of the knowledge base becomes clearer
through practical O&M question-answering scenarios.
Application cases of operations knowledge bases
Knowledge bases based on LLMs are widely used in the operations field. Unlike traditional
knowledge bases that can only retrieve relevant documents or data—requiring users to further
read, analyze, and understand them—a knowledge base built on an LLM can directly understand
the user’s question and, combined with existing documents, analyze, summarize, and provide

operational knowledge, the chapter now moves to another daily O&M workflow: ticket handling.
In this context, LLM agents can help summarize ticket information, interpret user requests, retrieve
relevant knowledge, call business systems, and guide tickets through the appropriate resolution
process.
Automating O&M ticket handling with LLM agents
Digital O&M services can help O&M teams provide various O&M services, such as release,
assurance, business continuity, and system reliability, to other internal IT functions and even
business teams, supporting enterprises in digital transformation and change. Intelligent O&M
tickets is a key component of digital O&M services.

chunks.content:
Chapter 7 251
Intelligent O&M tickets bring together several capabilities discussed earlier in the chapter:
knowledge retrieval, business-context understanding, tool use, and workflow automation. To
understand how LLM agents can improve ticket handling, it is useful to first look at the role
tickets play in O&M workflows, then examine why general-purpose LLMs are not sufficient on
their own, and finally see how an agent-based framework can support practical ticket processing.
The role of intelligent O&M tickets
O&M ticket management is an important part of O&M services and a commonly used basic service
within O&M organizations. In the O&M service process, if users want to know the progress and
handling comments after submitting an incident ticket, they need to check the solution status and
handling comments of the nodes on the ticket details page. When O&M engineers are handling
tickets, they need to view the basic information of the incident ticket submitted by the user or
review the ticket information processed by previous nodes, which requires looking at the event’s
basic information fields, the solution status, and the handling comments of previous nodes.
O&M managers, when wanting to know the solution status and solutions of different nodes for
an incident ticket, need to check the form information of different nodes. For all users of the ticket
management process, if they need to understand the overview information of an incident ticket,
they all need to spend time viewing the relevant form fields. Existing O&M service management
tools lack a way for users to quickly grasp ticket information.
Tools by capability
LLM-assisted ticket handling is usually integrated with existing IT service manage -
ment, incident management, or on-call platforms. Common platforms include Jira
Service Management, ServiceNow, PagerDuty, and Opsgenie. In these environments,
LLM agents can help summarize ticket content, classify incidents, retrieve relevant
knowledge-base articles, suggest next steps, call internal APIs, and route tickets to
the right team or workflow.
The ticketing platform remains the system of record, while the LLM agent provides an
intelligence layer for understanding, summarizing, and acting on ticket information.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 252
For example, an intelligent O&M ticketing platform can use an agent-based workflow to summarize
ticket status, progress, and handling context for different stakeholders, as shown in Figure 7.18.
Figure 7.18: An intelligent O&M ticketing platform’s function page
This kind of ticket summarization requires more than text generation. The system must understand
ticket fields, user roles, business rules, historical context, and available APIs, which is why the
technical pathway relies on agent-based orchestration.

Technical pathways for building intelligent O&M ticketing
Building intelligent O&M ticket workflows requires more than adding an LLM to an existing
ticketing system. The system must understand business-specific ticket content, retrieve relevant
operational knowledge, call internal APIs, and produce stable outputs that different users can
trust. The following discussion first examines the technical challenges involved, then introduces
an agent-based framework for handling them.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 253
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 253
Challenges of current O&M LLM technology
In the design of intelligent O&M tickets, empowering O&M businesses with LLM-related
technologies requires solving two problems: first, how to teach LLMs to handle actual O&M
business, and second, how to balance stability and flexibility in the models. The main challenge
in choosing a technical path is that LLMs only possess general capabilities and are difficult to
use directly for specific business problems.
This challenge is easier to see in business-service scenarios where the model must not only
understand the user’s request, but also call internal systems and follow organization-specific
rules. Taking the operator’s O&M customer service scenario as an example, when a customer
inquires, such as “My phone number is 130XXXXXXXX, my name is John Doe, and the last six
digits of my ID are 000000. Please check my phone bill,” the typical reply from a general-purpose
GPT model is shown in Figure 7.19.
Figure 7.19: Example of a generic GPT reply
A general LLM can understand concepts such as phone numbers and names, and can recognize the
user’s need to query their phone bill, but does not yet possess the professional business capabilities
of an operator O&M customer service agent. Therefore, in applying LLMs to actual O&M business,
the core issue is how to cultivate their ability to solve real O&M business problems based on their
general knowledge. In intelligent O&M ticket scenarios, intelligent agent technology can endow
LLMs with the ability to execute business logic and call tools.
Applying LLMs in Intelligent Operations and Maintenance 254
In addition, the advantage of LLMs lies in their outstanding generalization ability, meaning they
can flexibly respond to different input information and process it accordingly. However, from a
technical standpoint, no LLM can guarantee solving all problems 100% of the time. Therefore,
in the intelligent O&M ticket scenario, rational system design is still required to ensure that the
LLM agent has both the stability and flexibility to handle problems.
An O&M LLM framework based on agent technology
Based on the intelligent O&M ticket scenario, YunZhiHui has designed an agent framework called
the multi-level API selector. The framework, as shown in Figure 7.20, mainly consists of four parts:
1. Pattern Recognition: Follows rule matching and executes the matched model according
to established logic
2. Semantic Retrieval: Establishes a preset ticket knowledge base, vectorizes the contents
of the ticket database and user requests via embedding, and retrieves based on vector
similarity
3. LLM Tool Selection: Used for situations that require calling external APIs. The LLM
determines, based on the user request and available API list, whether to use an external
API and which API to use.

chunks.heading: Chapter 7 253
chunks.content:
4. Output results: Generate the final result based on the API return results and the user’s
request content
Figure 7.20: Multi-level API selector framework
The multi-level API selector provides a basic structure for routing requests and calling tools, but
more complex ticket scenarios often require multi-step reasoning, review, memory, and planning.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 7 255
chunks.content:
Chapter 7 255
The traditional multi-level API selector framework only involves single-step reasoning (tool
selection, generating the final result), making it unable to support complex logical reasoning
scenarios, such as multi-path chain reasoning, dual-Agent review, tree-structured reasoning,
etc. The multi-path chain reasoning technique of this framework is derived from the paper Self-
Consistency Improves Chain Of Thought Reasoning In Language Models, which enhances the Agent’s
self-consistency and thereby improves performance by using multiple reasoning paths with the
same logic but different temperature coefficients. The dual-Agent review technique is based on
the paper Communicative Agents for Software Development, which sets up two Agents with different
behavioral logics to discuss the same task and takes the agreed-upon conclusion as the output,
reducing hallucinations and intellectual limitations of a single Agent. Tree-structured reasoning
originates from the paper Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with LLMs and is suitable
for tree-based reasoning scenarios, supporting inference methods such as breadth-first search.
When dealing with scenarios that may involve complex reasoning logic, Yunzhihui surveyed the
existing Agent frameworks LangFlow and Flowise at the initial stage of framework design. It was
found that both frameworks are essentially graphical interfaces for LangChain, without additional
abstraction or encapsulation. For non-developers (industry experts), LangFlow and Flowise
have made many simplifications to lower the usage threshold, leading to unsatisfactory output
results. For developers, the cost reduction brought by framework simplification is limited, while
the inflexibility of the frameworks adds extra workload. The core issue with these frameworks
is that they fail to meet the needs of their target users. Developers want to lower development
costs while solving real-world problems, whereas non-developers hope to be able to build usable
applications independently without development skills.
Based on this, Yunzhihui designed an iterative version of the Agent framework, which is
composed of Agent, Planning, PlanUnit, Profile, Memory, and Action modules. Among them,
the Agent component can be used to complete complex tasks, such as complaint ticket processing
tasks. The Planning component is responsible for performing specific logic (such as CoT, ReAct);
the logic execution flow of each Planning can be viewed as a directed graph—single-path chain
reasoning, multi-path chain reasoning, tree reasoning, etc. are all subgraphs of the directed graph.
The PlanUnit component is responsible for executing single-step logic; it is a node in the Planning
directed graph, composed of Profile, Memory, Action, and other parts. The Profile component is

chunks.heading: Chapter 7 255
chunks.content:
used to set up the Agent’s role-playing, the Memory component is responsible for information
management, including the management and retrieval of context history information, as well
as vector recall from external knowledge bases based on user queries. The Action component is
responsible for external API management.

The architecture of the Agent framework is shown in Figure 7.21.
Figure 7.21: Architecture of the Agent framework
With this framework in place, the ticketing system can move from simple information retrieval
to role-aware ticket summarization and guided handling.
Application case of intelligent O&M ticketing
The intelligent ticket Agent will summarize the ticket based on the current ticket information and
user identity, combined with business logic, and display the summary in an internal operations
assistant interface. The case shown in Figure 7.22 demonstrates a fault report ticket related to
a drive failure. When processing this fault ticket, the intelligent ticket Agent analyzes the fault
content using its own O&M knowledge and summarizes information such as the fault situation
and handling progress based on relevant ticket fields.
